evidence.title: How They Survive (II)
evidence.author: Barany, Zoltan
excerpts: Abstract This chapter discusses key aspects of the state’s role in and with the security sector, such as relations with police and other law enforcement agencies, institutional arrangements and reforms, personnel and training, budget, and the scourge of corruption.
In the second half, the focus shifts to the unique characteristics of primary case study states and the professionalism of their security organizations.
We also evaluate the concern of “creeping militarization,” the notion that the appearance and operations of some security forces approximate those of regular military units.
The last section deals with security assistance and China’s increasing pressure on unarmed countries.

evidence.title: How They Survive (I)
evidence.author: Barany, Zoltan
excerpts: Abstract How is the sovereignty of states without armies protected?
How have states without armies dealt with threats to their external security without an army of their own?
The first section examines how unarmed states benefit from the post-World War II international system that requires peaceful settlement of disputes.
In the second part, we look at the alliances as well as regional and bilateral links that demilitarized states maintain.
The third portion focuses on the domestic and interstate conflicts and transnational challenges demilitarized states have experienced and resolved.

This chapter demonstrates that while active participation in international organizations and securing the protection of a regional hegemon shields demilitarized states though ultimately they remain vulnerable to the pressures of stronger, armed countries.

evidence.title: Cactus
excerpts: A cactus (pl.: cacti, cactuses, or less commonly, cactus) is a member of the plant family Cactaceae (), a family of the order Caryophyllales comprising about 131-140 genera with some 1,866 up to 2000+ known species.
The word cactus derives, through Latin, from the Ancient Greek word κάκτος (káktos), a name originally used by Theophrastus for a spiny plant whose identity is now not certain.
They are native to the Americas, ranging from Patagonia in the south to parts of western Canada in the north, with the exception of Rhipsalis baccifera, which is also found in Africa and Sri Lanka.
Cacti are adapted to live in very dry environments, including the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth.
Because of this, cacti show many adaptations to conserve water.
For example, almost all cacti are succulents, meaning they have thickened, fleshy organs adapted to store water.
Unlike many other succulents, the stem is the only part of most cacti where water storage takes place.
Most species of cacti have lost true leaves, retaining only spines, which are highly modified leaves.
As well as defending against herbivores, spines help prevent water loss by reducing air flow close to the cactus and providing some shade.
In the absence of true leaves, cacti's enlarged stems carry out photosynthesis.
Cactus spines are produced from specialized structures called areoles, a kind of highly reduced branch.
As well as spines, areoles give rise to flowers, which are usually tubular and multipetaled.

evidence.title: Evolution (Baxter novel)
excerpts: Evolution is a collection of short stories that work together to form an episodic science fiction novel by author Stephen Baxter.

It follows 565 million years of human evolution, from shrewlike mammals 65 million years in the past to the ultimate fate of humanity and its descendants, both biological and non-biological, 500 million years in the future.

evidence.title: Gregory Horror Show
excerpts: Gregory Horror Show (stylized in all caps) is a Japanese CGI anime interstitial television series created by Naomi Iwata and broadcast on select TV Asahi stations between October 1, 1999, and June 30, 2001.
The series revolves around the mysterious hotel named Gregory House, where lost souls often end up, run by an old mouse named Gregory.
The series is noted for its unusual papercraft-themed art style (similar to the one used in Pecola) and surreal tone.

evidence.title: List of plants with symbolism
excerpts: Various folk cultures and traditions assign symbolic meanings to plants.
Although these are no longer commonly understood by populations that are increasingly divorced from their rural traditions, some meanings survive.
In addition, these meanings are alluded to in older pictures, songs and writings.
New symbols have also arisen: one of the most known in the United Kingdom is the red poppy as a symbol of remembrance of the fallen in war.
